newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Solana begins tough Moscow talks on NATO growth.
newsitem.headline: Solana begins tough Moscow talks on NATO growth.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana met Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Monday for what both sides expect to be tough talks on the alliance's plans to take in new members from eastern and central Europe.
"The talks will last five hours, including a lunch," a spokesman for the NATO representative office in Moscow, John Lough, told Reuters by telephone.
The talks were being held at a state guest house outside Moscow. The precise venue was not disclosed.
Solana's visit is aimed at easing Russia's fears that an enlarged NATO would threaten its security and make new divisions in Europe.
He is expected to offer some form of permanent consultative forum between the former Cold War foes, greater flexibility on arms control issues and more economic assistance.

But both sides played down chances of a breakthrough in the long dispute, particularly in the absence of President Boris Yeltsin, who is in hospital with pneumonia. A Kremlin spokesman said no news of his condition was expected till later on Monday.

"Solana faces a hard task -- to convince his eastern neighbour that taking former socialist countries into NATO does not threaten its security and strengthens stability in Europe," Russia's NTV commercial television said.

"The Russian leader's absence from the Kremlin disturbs Western representatives. In their opinion, neither Primakov...or anyone else can independently take decisions determining what Russia and all Europe will be like in the next century."
In a sign of the sensitivity of the talks, Solana was kept away from reporters and whisked into central Moscow on Sunday. No news conference, or even photo opportunity, is scheduled.
Lough said Solana would fly back to Brussels later on Monday.

NATO's proposed expansion is again centre stage in Moscow after a year in which attention focused first on July's presidential election, which Yeltsin won, and then on his heart problems, which kept him out of the Kremlin until December 23.

Russia launched a new diplomatic offensive against the alliance's plans after Yeltsin returned to the Kremlin and ordered the Foreign Ministry to start drawing up a set of possible responses to an enlarged NATO.

Diplomats say Russia appears intent on delaying enlargement, limiting the number of countries that join NATO and seeking as many concessions as possible over one of the few issues which unites Russian politicians across the political spectrum.
But time is running out for reaching an understanding before a July summit in Madrid at which NATO is expected to issue invitations to the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland.
NATO officials said Solana would bring no essentially new thinking but ideas had been developed for flexibility on arms control, military cooperation and more economic aid.

The NATO officials hoped there was room for progress on two issues which Moscow had singled out as important -- the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) accord, which Moscow says is outdated, and creation of a permanent consultation mechanism.
They said the latter could cover issues ranging from nuclear proliferation, terrorism, anti-missile defence systems and international crime.
It was far from certain that such proposals would meet Russia's demands for a structure giving it a say in all issues covering its "vital interests."

Neither side expected immediate agreement but each hoped to lay the groundwork for further talks. "No one is anticipating changes in either position at this stage, but Solana wants to get the ball rolling," a NATO diplomat said.
